lessons.title: Russia in 1894: Economy and Society
lessons.description: Industrial growth, peasant villages and city slums under the last Tsar's vast empire.
spec_references: living and working conditions in cities and villages
key_topics: Geography and population of the Russian Empire in 1894
Witte's industrialisation drive and Trans-Siberian Railway
Living conditions in St Petersburg and Moscow factories
Peasant life: the mir, the village commune and rural poverty
Class structure: nobility, bourgeoisie, proletariat, peasantry
anticipated_misconceptions: Russia was uniformly poor and pre-industrial — in fact Witte's reforms made it the world's fourth largest industrial economy by 1914, but extremely uneven.
All peasants owned their land after 1861 — many were in heavy debt to the state for 'redemption payments' on land they had been freed onto.

lessons.title: Nicholas II's Autocracy and Opposition
lessons.description: The court, Okhrana, Orthodox Church and the revolutionary parties challenging Tsarist rule.
spec_references: Nicholas II's autocracy and the court
key_topics: The principles of Tsarist autocracy: 'Orthodoxy, Autocracy, Nationality'
The court, the Tsarina and the role of the Romanov family
The Okhrana (secret police) and political repression
Liberal opposition: the Kadets and Octobrists
Revolutionary opposition: Social Revolutionaries vs Social Democrats (Bolsheviks/Mensheviks split 1903)
anticipated_misconceptions: All revolutionaries were Bolsheviks — there were several rival groups and the Bolsheviks were a small faction until 1917.
Nicholas II personally chose to be a tyrant — he believed autocracy was a sacred religious duty inherited from his father.
key_dates: 1898 — Russian Social Democratic Labour Party founded
1903 — Bolshevik/Menshevik split at the Second Party Congress

lessons.title: The 1905 Revolution and October Manifesto
lessons.description: Bloody Sunday, soviets and a Tsar forced to grant a parliament he did not want.
key_topics: The Russo-Japanese War 1904-05 and military humiliation
Bloody Sunday — Father Gapon and the Winter Palace, January 1905
Spread of strikes, mutinies (Battleship Potemkin) and the St Petersburg Soviet
The October Manifesto: civil rights, the Duma, legal political parties
Why the autocracy survived: army loyalty, divided opposition, concessions
anticipated_misconceptions: Bloody Sunday marchers wanted to overthrow the Tsar — they were a peaceful procession carrying icons and a petition asking him to help them.
The October Manifesto was a willing reform — Nicholas signed it under duress and resented it for the rest of his reign.

lessons.title: Stolypin, the Dumas and Reform to 1914
lessons.description: Land reform, the noose, four Dumas and a regime stuck between repression and modernisation.
spec_references: the impact of, and reactions to, attempts to reform Russia up to 1914
Stolypin's policies – land reform, industry and use of oppression
key_topics: The Fundamental Laws (1906) and limits on the Duma's power
The four Dumas 1906-1917: dissolved, narrowed, ignored
Stolypin's land reform — the wager on the strong peasants
'Stolypin's necktie': field court martials and political hangings
Industrial growth and continuing urban unrest by 1914 (Lena Goldfields massacre 1912)
anticipated_misconceptions: The Dumas were like a modern parliament — they had very limited powers and the Tsar dismissed them whenever they criticised him.
Stolypin was just a brutal hangman — he combined repression with the most ambitious agricultural reform of the period; historians debate whether his death in 1911 doomed Tsardom.

lessons.title: The First World War and the Fall of the Tsar
lessons.description: Defeats, food queues, Rasputin and the abdication of Nicholas II in March 1917.
spec_references: The First World War: the impact of military defeats on Tsarist government
social and economic effects of war on cities and the countryside
unpopularity of the Romanovs, including the role of Rasputin
key_topics: Initial patriotic enthusiasm and rapid military disaster — Tannenberg, Masurian Lakes
Nicholas takes personal command at the front (Sept 1915) — political consequences
Alexandra, Rasputin and the discrediting of the dynasty
Inflation, food and fuel shortages in Petrograd; rural conscription crisis
February Revolution: bread riots, Petrograd garrison mutiny, abdication
anticipated_misconceptions: Nicholas II was overthrown by the Bolsheviks — he abdicated in March 1917 after the spontaneous February Revolution; the Bolsheviks did not seize power until October.
Rasputin ran the country — his real influence was modest, but the perception of his hold over Alexandra destroyed public trust in the dynasty.
key_dates: Aug 1914 — Russia enters First World War

lessons.title: The Provisional Government's Crisis
lessons.description: Dual Power, Order Number 1 and a government undone by war, land and bread.
spec_references: The Provisional Government: its failure to deal with Russia's social, economic and military problems
key_topics: Dual Power: Provisional Government and Petrograd Soviet
Order Number 1 and the collapse of military discipline
Continuation of the war — the disastrous June Offensive 1917
Land seizures by peasants; food shortages worsen
The Kornilov Affair (August 1917) and the rearming of the Bolsheviks
anticipated_misconceptions: The Provisional Government was elected — it was self-appointed from the old Duma and never had a popular mandate; it kept postponing Constituent Assembly elections.
It was always doomed — historians debate whether continuing the war was the fatal choice; ending it might have saved it.
key_dates: Mar 1917 — Order Number 1 issued by Petrograd Soviet

lessons.title: Lenin, Trotsky and the October Revolution
lessons.description: April Theses, the growth of the Bolsheviks and Red Guards storming the Winter Palace.
key_topics: Lenin's return in the sealed train; the April Theses ('Peace, Land, Bread')
Trotsky's defection from the Mensheviks; chairing the Petrograd Soviet
Bolshevik organisation: discipline, slogans, growing soviet majorities
The October seizure of power: Military Revolutionary Committee, Winter Palace, Soviet Congress
Why the Bolsheviks won in 1917: weakness of opponents vs strength of party
anticipated_misconceptions: The October Revolution was a mass uprising — it was a tightly planned coup by a few thousand Red Guards and sailors, although it had wider soviet support.
It happened in November — old-style Russian calendar dates it October; new-style November. Both names are correct.
key_dates: Apr 1917 — Lenin returns to Russia; April Theses

lessons.title: Lenin in Power: Brest-Litovsk, Cheka and Civil War
lessons.description: First decrees, a brutal peace with Germany and the secret police that crushed dissent.
spec_references: the impact of Lenin's dictatorship: the end of the First World War
causes, nature and consequences of the Civil War and Bolshevik success
key_topics: Early Bolshevik decrees: Land, Peace, Workers' Control, nationalisation
Constituent Assembly elections (Nov 1917) and dispersal (Jan 1918)
Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (Mar 1918): Russia leaves the war, huge territorial losses
The Cheka — Dzerzhinsky's secret police and the Red Terror
Civil War 1918-21: Reds vs Whites and Greens; foreign intervention; Trotsky's Red Army; murder of the Romanovs (1918); use of propaganda
Why the Reds won — interior lines, unity, leadership, divided Whites
anticipated_misconceptions: The Cheka was the same as the NKVD — different organisations from different decades; the Cheka came first (1917-22), the NKVD took over secret police functions under Stalin in the 1930s.
The Whites were a single army — they were several disconnected forces (Denikin, Kolchak, Yudenich, Wrangel) which never coordinated effectively.
key_dates: Jul 1918 — Romanov family murdered at Ekaterinburg

lessons.title: War Communism, Kronstadt and the NEP
lessons.description: Grain requisitioning, sailors in revolt and Lenin's strategic retreat to a mixed economy.
spec_references: Social and economic developments: War Communism
the achievements of Lenin and Trotsky
key_topics: War Communism (1918-21): grain requisitioning, banned private trade, militarised labour
Famine 1921-22 and the collapse of industrial output
The Kronstadt Rising (March 1921) — sailors who had once been the 'pride of the revolution' demand reform; Trotsky orders the Red Army to crush them
The Tenth Party Congress and the New Economic Policy: peasants pay tax in kind, small private businesses legal again
NEP debate: 'tactical retreat' or betrayal of socialism? Achievements and limits of Lenin and Trotsky's leadership
anticipated_misconceptions: The NEP was Lenin abandoning communism — he saw it as a temporary retreat; the political dictatorship of the party was reinforced even as economic life relaxed.
Kronstadt was crushed by Tsarist enemies — those sailors had been Bolshevik heroes in 1917; Lenin and Trotsky put down their own former supporters.
key_dates: Mar 1921 — Kronstadt Rising; Tenth Party Congress; NEP introduced

lessons.title: The Power Struggle to Succeed Lenin
lessons.description: Lenin's testament, Stalin's machine politics and the eclipse of Trotsky 1924-1929.
spec_references: Stalin the dictator: the power struggle to succeed Lenin
the control of the Communist party over government
key_topics: Lenin's death (January 1924) and the suppression of his Testament
Contenders: Trotsky, Stalin, Zinoviev, Kamenev, Bukharin
Stalin's role as General Secretary: control of party appointments
Ideological clashes: Permanent Revolution (Trotsky) vs Socialism in One Country (Stalin)
Tactical alliances and betrayals; expulsion of Trotsky (1929); the 'right deviation' and Bukharin's defeat (1929)
anticipated_misconceptions: Trotsky was the obvious heir — many in 1924 expected this, but Stalin's bureaucratic position outmanoeuvred him.
Stalin was always the front-runner — he was widely underestimated as a 'grey blur' until it was too late to stop him.
key_dates: 1928-1929 — Defeat of the Right; Stalin emerges supreme

lessons.title: Collectivisation and the War on the Kulaks
lessons.description: Forced grain seizures, dekulakisation and the Ukrainian famine of 1932-33.
spec_references: Stalin's modernisation of the USSR: collectivisation
social and economic consequences for Kulaks
key_topics: End of the NEP and the 'Great Turn' of 1928
How collectivisation worked: kolkhoz, sovkhoz, MTS (machine tractor stations)
Dekulakisation — deportation, exile, execution of better-off peasants
Resistance: peasants slaughtering livestock; passive sabotage
The Ukrainian famine (Holodomor) 1932-33; debates over intent and scale
anticipated_misconceptions: All kulaks were rich farmers — the label was applied very loosely; many were ordinary peasants targeted because they resisted or because quotas had to be filled.
Collectivisation made Soviet agriculture more efficient — Soviet grain output did not regain 1928 levels for decades; the gain was political control, not productivity.
key_dates: 1928 — End of the NEP; collectivisation begins
1932-1933 — Famine in Ukraine, Kazakhstan and elsewhere

lessons.title: The Five Year Plans and Soviet Society
lessons.description: Magnitogorsk, Stakhanovites, Soviet women and the human cost of headline targets.
spec_references: social and economic consequences for city dwellers, women, professional and industrial workers
key_topics: Aims of the Five Year Plans: heavy industry, autarky, war preparation
First (1928-32), Second (1933-37), Third (1938-41) Plans — what each prioritised
Showcase projects: Magnitogorsk, Dnieper Dam, Moscow Metro, White Sea Canal
Workers' lives: Stakhanovism, internal passports, harsh labour discipline
Soviet women: drawn into the workforce; education and welfare gains; double burden at home
Were the Plans a success? Headline output vs quality, accidents and gulag labour
anticipated_misconceptions: The Five Year Plans simply succeeded — they hit headline tonnage targets but at huge social cost, with poor quality goods and gulag labour disguised in the totals; examiner reports flag students who skip this.
Stalin personally caused the success — millions of ordinary workers, foreign engineers and forced labourers built the projects; Stalin set the targets.
key_dates: 1938-1941 — Third Five Year Plan (interrupted by war)

lessons.title: Terror, Purges and the Cult of Stalin
lessons.description: Show trials, the NKVD, gulag camps, censorship and the propaganda image of a great leader.
key_topics: Trigger: Kirov's murder (December 1934)
Show trials of the Old Bolsheviks (1936-38): Zinoviev, Kamenev, Bukharin
Purge of the Red Army — Tukhachevsky and the officer corps
The NKVD under Yagoda, Yezhov and Beria; the gulag system
Censorship, Socialist Realism and the cult of personality (paintings, statues, school textbooks)
Why? Historiography: totalitarian school (Conquest) — Stalin's personal will; revisionist (Fitzpatrick, Getty) — pressure from below and bureaucratic chaos
anticipated_misconceptions: Only old Bolsheviks were purged — millions of ordinary workers, peasants, Poles, Germans and minority nationalities were swept up too.
Everyone was secretly opposed to Stalin — many genuinely believed in him; the cult was effective precisely because much of the propaganda was internalised.
key_dates: 1936-1938 — Great Terror peak; Moscow show trials
1937 — Purge of Red Army officer corps

lessons.title: The Great Patriotic War, 1941-1945
lessons.description: Operation Barbarossa, Stalingrad, evacuation of industry and the cost of victory.
spec_references: Impact of the Second World War: Stalin's wartime leadership
political, economic and social problems caused by the Great Patriotic War up to 1945
key_topics: Nazi-Soviet Pact (1939) and Stalin's miscalculation
Operation Barbarossa (June 1941) — initial catastrophe; Stalin's withdrawal and return
Mobilising the home front: evacuation of factories east of the Urals; women in industry
The siege of Leningrad; Battle of Stalingrad (1942-43); Battle of Kursk (1943)
Wartime use of patriotism, the Orthodox Church and the relaxation/tightening of repression
Costs by 1945: c.27 million Soviet dead, devastated cities, vast expansion of Soviet power
anticipated_misconceptions: Stalin was always a brilliant wartime leader — he was paralysed in the first week of Barbarossa and the early purge of officers worsened the disaster.
The USSR won because of Allied aid alone — Lend-Lease mattered, but the relocation of industry and Soviet manpower were decisive; historians debate the balance.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat 'the Russian Revolution' as a single event in October 1917, ignoring the spontaneous February Revolution that overthrew the Tsar eight months earlier. They then credit the Bolsheviks with overthrowing Nicholas II.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA principal examiner reports on 8145/1A/C Russia period study; Historical Association A-level topic guide on Russia and the USSR

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume the Provisional Government was elected and democratic. In fact it was self-appointed from the old Duma's Progressive Bloc, lacked any popular mandate, and kept postponing the Constituent Assembly elections that would have given it one.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA sample mark scheme commentary for 8145/1A/C; History Today archive on Lenin and the Russian Revolution

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students conflate the Cheka (Lenin's secret police, 1917-22) with the NKVD (Stalin-era secret police that ran the Great Terror in 1936-38). They treat them as one continuous body and miss the institutional change between Lenin's and Stalin's regimes.
common_misconceptions.source: Historical Association resource 'Stalin, Propaganda and Soviet Society during the Great Terror'; History Today archive on the purges

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students assert the Plans 'succeeded because Stalin was a great leader'. AQA examiner commentary repeatedly flags that top-band answers must weigh headline tonnage gains against quality failures, gulag labour hidden in the figures, and the human cost of collectivisation that fed the cities.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA principal examiner commentary on 12-mark bullet-format judgement questions; Historical Association film 'Stalin — The Early Soviet Economy and the Preparation for War'

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students think 'kulak' meant 'rich peasant' in any consistent sense. In practice the label was applied loosely and politically — anyone resisting collectivisation could be branded a kulak, including ordinary peasants with one extra cow.
common_misconceptions.source: Historical Association A-level Russia and the USSR topic guide; History Today archive on collectivisation

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students describe October 1917 as a mass popular uprising. It was a tightly planned coup by a few thousand armed workers, soldiers and sailors organised by Trotsky's Military Revolutionary Committee, even if it had wider soviet support.
common_misconceptions.source: History Today archive 'The Russian Revolution in Today's Perspective'; AQA sample interpretations booklet for 8145/1A/C

examiner_signals.signal: Top-band 12-mark bullet-format essays on Russia reach a substantiated overall judgement (e.g. 'collectivisation did more than the Terror to entrench Stalin's power because…') rather than describing both bullets in turn. Examiner reports repeatedly flag the missing judgement step.
examiner_signals.source: AQA principal examiner commentary on 8145/1A/C Q6

examiner_signals.signal: On the 4-mark 'why interpretations differ' question, students lose marks when they describe what each interpretation says rather than explaining why — purpose, time of writing, evidence used, perspective of the historian.

The 8-mark 'how convincing' question rewards students who use specific contextual knowledge to test the interpretation, not who repeat phrases from it. Russia rewards precise dates (Aug 1942, Mar 1921), names (Yezhov, Bukharin) and statistics where possible.
examiner_signals.source: AQA sample mark scheme for 8145/1A/C Q3

examiner_signals.signal: On 8-mark 'in what ways' (effects) questions, top answers explain a chain of consequences rather than listing changes — e.g. War Communism caused famine which caused Kronstadt which caused the NEP.

Russia interpretations frequently come from contrasting authors — Mensheviks vs Bolsheviks, émigré vs Soviet historians, totalitarian school vs revisionists. Top answers name or characterise the school of thought rather than just the individual.
examiner_signals.source: AQA sample interpretations booklet for 8145/1A/C; Historical Association resource on Stalinism

topic_weighting_notes: Across past Paper 1A/C question papers, the option is balanced across the three parts. Students are expected to be able to write substantively on the end of Tsardom, Lenin's regime and Stalin's regime — single-part revision strategies have repeatedly underperformed.
1917 (the two revolutions and their aftermath) is the most recurrent focus of interpretation questions; students need to be confident on causes and consequences of both February and October.

Stalin's modernisation (Plans + collectivisation) and the Terror are both heavily examined — these are the highest-leverage areas in Part 3 and reward connected understanding (industrialisation needed grain → forced collectivisation; Plans needed labour → gulag).
The Great Patriotic War tends to feature in 8-mark or 12-mark questions on Stalin's leadership rather than as a standalone narrative; cover it but tie it back to the consolidation of Stalin's rule.

key_dates_and_events.event: Bloody Sunday — Father Gapon's peaceful petition is fired on outside the Winter Palace; trigger for the 1905 Revolution.
key_dates_and_events.significance: Shatters the myth of the 'good Tsar' and starts a year of mutinies, strikes and soviets. Forces the October Manifesto.

key_dates_and_events.event: October Manifesto — Nicholas II concedes a Duma, civil rights and legal political parties.
key_dates_and_events.significance: Saves the autocracy in the short term but creates the constitutional tension that defines 1906-1917.

key_dates_and_events.event: February Revolution and abdication of Nicholas II.
key_dates_and_events.significance: Ends 300 years of Romanov rule. Creates Dual Power between the Provisional Government and Petrograd Soviet.

key_dates_and_events.event: October Revolution — Bolshevik seizure of power in Petrograd.
key_dates_and_events.significance: First successful Marxist revolution. Begins 74 years of Communist rule. Triggers Civil War and intervention.
Russia loses Ukraine, the Baltic, Finland and Poland but exits the First World War — letting Lenin focus on consolidating power.

key_dates_and_events.event: Kronstadt Rising and Tenth Party Congress; introduction of the NEP.
key_dates_and_events.significance: Marks the limit of War Communism and the start of Lenin's tactical retreat. Ban on factions inside the party formalises one-party dictatorship.
Begins the five-year power struggle Stalin will eventually win. Lenin's Testament is suppressed.

key_dates_and_events.event: First Five Year Plan and the launch of forced collectivisation.
key_dates_and_events.significance: Ends the NEP; transforms the Soviet economy and rural society at huge human cost.

key_dates_and_events.event: Murder of Sergei Kirov in Leningrad.
key_dates_and_events.significance: Used by Stalin as the trigger for the Great Terror. Kirov's killer's motives still debated.

key_dates_and_events.event: Show trials of the Old Bolsheviks; peak of the Great Terror.
key_dates_and_events.significance: Eliminates Stalin's surviving rivals and remoulds the party and Red Army into instruments of his personal rule.

key_dates_and_events.event: Operation Barbarossa — Nazi invasion of the USSR.
key_dates_and_events.significance: Catches Stalin off guard. Leads to the Great Patriotic War and Soviet emergence as a superpower.

key_dates_and_events.event: Surrender of German 6th Army at Stalingrad.
key_dates_and_events.significance: Turning point of the Eastern Front. Cements Stalin's wartime authority and the propaganda narrative of victory.

historiography_notes.view: Treats the October Revolution as a coup imposed by a small fanatical party rather than a mass revolution. Sees 1917-1991 as a single tragic experiment rooted in Lenin's authoritarianism.
historiography_notes.use_for_students: Useful framing for 'why convincing' interpretation questions when the source is critical of the Bolsheviks — students can name the tradition the writer is drawing on.

historiography_notes.view: Presents 1917 as the inevitable triumph of the working class led by the Bolshevik vanguard. Stalin's Plans are heroic modernisation; the Purges are minimised or reframed as a defence of socialism.
historiography_notes.use_for_students: Recognise it in older Soviet-era sources or memoirs. Top-band answers can flag this as a reason an interpretation differs (purpose, time of writing).

historiography_notes.view: Argues Stalin's rule was driven by a single tyrant's will. The Terror and famine were deliberately engineered top-down. Collectivisation and the Purges are continuous with Lenin's authoritarianism.
historiography_notes.use_for_students: The default 'Stalin caused everything' interpretation. Useful for students answering 'how convincing' on a Stalin-as-monster source.

historiography_notes.school: Revisionist (e.g. Sheila Fitzpatrick, J. Arch Getty)
historiography_notes.view: Argues the Terror grew partly out of bureaucratic chaos, denunciations from below, and conflict between centre and provinces — not just Stalin's personal will. Stresses that ordinary Soviet citizens often supported the regime.
historiography_notes.use_for_students: A more recent counterweight. Strong students can contrast it with Conquest to explain why interpretations of the 1930s differ.

pedagogical_notes.note: Front-load the 1917 timeline. Students need a secure grasp of February (peaceful, urban, women on International Women's Day, Tsar abdicates) vs October (planned coup by Bolsheviks against the Provisional Government) before they can interpret sources or write narratives. Use a single dual-column timeline they re-revisit each lesson.
pedagogical_notes.source: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools — pre-teaching disciplinary vocabulary; AQA examiner reports flagging 1917 confusion.

pedagogical_notes.note: Teach the Stalin-era topics as connected systems rather than separate units: Plans need grain → collectivisation → famine; Plans need labour → Terror → gulag → industrial output. Examiner reports praise students who explain chains of consequence rather than listing.
pedagogical_notes.source: Cambridge Assessment research on comparative judgement; AQA examiner commentary on 12-mark essays.

pedagogical_notes.note: Use parallel quotes from a totalitarian-school historian (e.g. Conquest on the Terror) and a revisionist (e.g. Fitzpatrick) early in the Stalin sequence. This gives students a working example of why interpretations differ that they can keep returning to.
pedagogical_notes.source: EEF Metacognition guidance on modelling expert thinking; Historical Association resource pack on Stalinism.

pedagogical_notes.note: Russia's interpretation booklets often pair a Menshevik with a Bolshevik, or an émigré historian with a Soviet writer. Drill the 'why differ' framework — purpose, evidence, time of writing, perspective — at every opportunity. Students who only know the events reach the lower bands.
pedagogical_notes.source: AQA sample interpretations booklet for 8145/1A/C; AQA principal examiner commentary on Q2.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Tsar Nicholas II
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Last Romanov Tsar (1894-1917). Devoted to autocracy as a religious duty, took personal command of the army in 1915, abdicated in February 1917, executed with his family in July 1918.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Tsarina Alexandra
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Empress of Russia. German-born, devoutly Orthodox; her reliance on Rasputin during the war discredited the dynasty in elite and popular opinion.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Sergei Witte
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Finance Minister 1892-1903; architect of pre-war industrialisation and the Trans-Siberian Railway. Drafted the October Manifesto in 1905.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Pyotr Stolypin
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Prime Minister 1906-1911. Combined repression ('Stolypin's necktie') with the most ambitious land reform of the Tsarist era. Assassinated 1911.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Grigori Rasputin
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Siberian holy man. Won influence over the royal family through his apparent ability to ease the haemophilia of Tsarevich Alexei. Murdered December 1916.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Alexander Kerensky
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Lawyer; sole figure in both the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet. Prime Minister from July 1917; overthrown by the Bolsheviks in October.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Vladimir Lenin
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Founder of the Bolsheviks; led the October Revolution; head of government 1917-1924. Author of the April Theses, architect of War Communism and the NEP.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Leon Trotsky
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Chair of the Petrograd Soviet 1917; planner of the October Revolution; founder of the Red Army; defeated in the succession struggle, exiled 1929, killed in Mexico 1940.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Felix Dzerzhinsky
key_individuals_and_groups.role: First head of the Cheka (1917-1922). Architect of the Red Terror.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Joseph Stalin
key_individuals_and_groups.role: General Secretary of the Communist Party from 1922; supreme leader from c. 1929 until his death in 1953. Drove collectivisation, the Five Year Plans, the Great Terror and Soviet leadership in the Great Patriotic War.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Nikolai Bukharin
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Leading Bolshevik intellectual and editor of Pravda. Defender of the NEP; defeated by Stalin in 1929 and shot after the third Moscow show trial in 1938.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Grigori Zinoviev and Lev Kamenev
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Old Bolsheviks; allied with Stalin against Trotsky in the 1920s, then turned on by Stalin and shot in the first Moscow show trial of 1936.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Nikolai Yezhov
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Head of the NKVD 1936-38; oversaw the peak of the Great Terror ('Yezhovshchina'). Replaced and shot by Stalin in 1940.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Lavrenti Beria
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Head of the NKVD from late 1938. Wound down the worst of the Yezhov purges and ran the secret police through the war and into Stalin's final years.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Marshal Georgy Zhukov
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Soviet commander; oversaw victories at Moscow, Stalingrad and Berlin. The most prominent Red Army general of the Great Patriotic War.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Bolsheviks
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Marxist faction founded by Lenin in 1903; renamed the Communist Party in 1918. The driving organisation of the October Revolution and the only legal party in the Soviet state.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Kulaks
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Better-off peasants; targeted for liquidation as a class during dekulakisation 1929-30. The label was applied loosely to almost any peasant resisting collectivisation.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Cheka and the NKVD
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Successive Soviet secret police. The Cheka (1917-22) ran the Red Terror under Lenin; the NKVD ran the gulag and the Great Terror under Stalin.
